title: Lynk Lab
text:
Problem
Lynk Lab started as a product at Lynk: a web app where a horseplayer could open a race, click on any horse, jockey or trainer, and ask questions in plain English. Behind it sat a cloud database with every race since 2012, a set of stored procedures and a chain of hosted language model calls that turned questions into SQL and SQL results into answers.
It worked, and it was accurate. However, it was expensive to run and impossible to share. Every question went through a login, a cloud function, a hosted model and a database, and the 2025 Kentucky Derby version sent roughly 175,000 characters of statistics (about 44,000 tokens) to the model with every single question before deciding whether it needed to query the database at all.
Problem statement: rebuild Lynk Lab so anyone can use it on a static web page, with no server, no login and no API key, while keeping the accuracy of the original and making each question cost a small fraction of the tokens.

For reference, the starts table alone is more than a quarter of a million rides and saddlings, so a question like “what does a $2 win bet on every Irad Ortiz Jr. ride for Steve Asmussen return?” is answered from 366 real races, not from a summary.
The AI predictions are the Lynk fundamental model’s win probabilities for this race, described in Handicapping Without the Tote. The model uses no betting odds and was trained only on races before 2025, so its view of the Derby is a genuine pre-race opinion. It liked Journalism most (16.3%) and had the eventual winner, Sovereignty, fourth at 8.4%.

title: Lynk Lab
text:
Approach

Everything runs in the browser
The analogy that comes to mind is moving a full stack application into the client. The two server pieces of the original app each have a browser equivalent:

The database becomes DuckDB-WASM. DuckDB is an analytical SQL engine, and its WebAssembly build runs inside the page. The tables above are downloaded once as Parquet files and every query, from a simple lookup to window functions over 273,455 rows, runs locally in milliseconds.
The hosted model becomes WebLLM. WebLLM runs a small open model (Qwen 2.5 with 1.5 or 3 billion parameters) on the visitor’s own graphics card through WebGPU. The first load downloads 1 to 2 GB of model weights into the browser’s cache. After that it starts in seconds and nothing leaves the machine.

There is no API key anywhere in the page, and nobody pays per question.


Three tiers: spend tokens only when they buy something
The original app sent everything to the model and let it figure out what to do. Lynk Lab does the reverse: it tries the cheapest correct path first and only involves the model when it adds value.





flowchart LR
  Q[Question] --> R{Tier 0 keyword router}
  R -- matches a tool --> T[Tested SQL tool]
  R -- no match --> L1{Tier 1 model picks a tool}
  L1 -- tool --> T
  L1 -- no tool fits --> L2[Tier 2 model writes SQL]
  L2 --> V[Validate: read-only, one SELECT, LIMIT 100]
  V -- error --> L2
  V --> D[(DuckDB in the browser)]
  T --> D
  D --> A[Model writes the answer from the returned rows only]







Tier 0, the router (zero tokens). Most questions people ask about a race are predictable: tell me about this horse, compare two horses, how does this jockey do in Grade 1 races, who has early speed, who changed riders. A keyword router recognizes these, resolves the horse, jockey and trainer names, and sends them straight to one of 14 tested SQL tools. The tools are ported from the original Lynk Lab queries (past performances, jockey and trainer records, the last-30-starts ROI, first-time riders, past Derby results) plus new ones such as the pace map and the AI value table.
Tier 1, tool choice. When the router does not recognize a question, the model sees a one-line description of each tool and the names in the race, and replies with a tiny JSON object naming the tool and its arguments.
Tier 2, text to SQL. When no tool fits (“which Derby trainers have won the most graded stakes since 2023?”), the model writes a SQL query from a verbose data dictionary: every column with its type, a plain-English description, its units and its real allowed values (the actual track conditions, race types, grades and track codes are read from the data when the page loads). It also gets five worked examples, including one that shows how to decline a question. The query is checked before it runs: one statement, read-only, no setting changes, wrapped in a 100-row limit. If DuckDB rejects it, the error goes back to the model for one retry, the same rewrite loop the original cloud function used.

When the data cannot answer, it says so. The dictionary ends with an explicit list of what the data does not contain (workouts, veterinary records, results after the Derby, races outside North America and so on). If a question needs any of it, the model must reply NO_DATA with a reason instead of writing SQL, and the app tells the user plainly that it cannot answer. A query that comes back empty gets the same honest message instead of a guess, and the model that writes the final answer is told exactly what the rows represent, so it cannot describe a table of all-surface speed figures as “muddy track” results.
In every case the final answer is written by the model from only the rows the query returned, capped at 15 rows and 12 columns. The model never does arithmetic. Win percentages, returns on investment and averages are computed by SQL, which is why the answers stay as accurate as the original’s.


Why it uses so few tokens

A typical question takes the Tier 0 path and about 400 to 600 tokens in total. The most expensive path (tool choice, SQL with the full dictionary, a retry and the answer) is around 6,000 tokens. In other words, the hardest question in Lynk Lab costs about a seventh of what the easiest question cost in the original, and it runs for free on the visitor’s own hardware.
Four design choices make that possible:

A verbose dictionary, but only where it is needed. The model gets a detailed description of the tables, not their contents, and only for the tables a question touches: a jockey question sends the starts and field descriptions, a question about a horse’s form sends past_performances. Detail is what makes small models write correct SQL, and selecting tables is what keeps that detail affordable. A dictionary costs the same no matter how many rows sit behind it, so the dataset can grow from one race to every race without the prompt growing.
The database does the math. Asking a language model to compute a win percentage from 10,000 rides is slow, expensive and error-prone. Asking it to write avg((finish = 1)::INT) is cheap and exact.
Small outputs. Tool choice is a short JSON object (80 tokens at most), SQL is capped at 220 tokens and answers at 200. Small models are fast when they write little.
Deterministic first. Anything a keyword router can do correctly, it does for free. The model is reserved for language: understanding unusual questions and writing the answer.



Suggestions that do not always pick the favorite
The original app had a feature I wanted to keep: ask for a bet suggestion and it would pick a horse at random in proportion to the AI’s win probabilities, then make the case for it. That way the suggestions follow the model without naming the same horse every time.
Lynk Lab keeps that logic and tempers it (probabilities are raised to the power 0.8 before sampling), so a longshot the model likes has a real chance to come up. For the chosen horse it pulls three facts at random from a pool (value against the morning line, recent speed figures, graded stakes wins, the jockey’s and trainer’s recent win rates), and recommends a bet type by price, following the original rules: a win bet and a key on top of exactas for horses at 10-1 or shorter, win and place with exacta and trifecta boxes for the middle of the pack, and place, show and underneath spots in trifectas and superfectas for longshots. Each suggestion says how likely that horse was to be picked. The question chips rotate too, filling their templates with different horses, jockeys and trainers after every answer.

title: Lynk Lab
text:
Results
On the questions I tested, every Tier 0 answer matched the chart data exactly, for example:

Sovereignty: five starts, two wins (the Street Sense and the Fountain of Youth) and second in the Florida Derby, with a best speed figure of 94.
Bob Baffert: 13 Derby starters since 2012 and four first-place finishes in the race-day charts. One of those, Medina Spirit in 2021, was later disqualified, and Mandaloun was declared the winner.
Flavien Prat: wins with 37.7% of his rides as the betting favorite, while a $2 win bet on those rides returned -14.2%.
Bill Mott: 124 wins from 844 starters at Churchill Downs.

Three consecutive bet suggestions picked Sovereignty, Final Gambit and Baeza, each with different supporting facts.

Verdict: moving the database and the model into the browser removed the server, the login and the per-question cost, and routing questions through tested SQL tools before the model cut the typical question from about 44,000 tokens to a few hundred without giving up accuracy.

title: Lynk Lab
text:
Limitations

A database bug I had to work around. While testing a named question (“how has Sovereignty run on wet tracks?”) I found that the DuckDB-WASM build I started on (1.29.0) silently dropped a horse = 'Sovereignty' filter when it was combined with a horse IN (subquery) filter, returning all 17 horses. Newer releases fix it, so the page now pins 1.32.0, and the tools and the data dictionary avoid that pattern entirely. The lesson is the same one as everywhere else in this project: check the numbers, not just the code.
It needs WebGPU for the AI. Chrome or Edge on a desktop with a recent graphics card runs the model well. Other browsers still get every built-in question with tables and written summaries, but not open-ended questions.
Small models are small. A 1.5 billion parameter model writes good SQL for clear questions and occasionally misreads an ambiguous one. The validation and retry loop catches errors that DuckDB rejects, but not a valid query that answers a slightly different question. Showing the SQL behind every answer keeps that visible.
Charts are race-day records. Results reflect the official order when the chart was published, so later rulings (such as the 2021 Medina Spirit disqualification) are not applied.
Two horses have no past performances. Luxor Cafe and Admire Daytona raced in Japan before the Derby, and the chart data only covers North American racing.
One race. The demo covers the 2025 Kentucky Derby. The architecture does not change for a full card or a full season. Only the data files grow.

title: Lynk Lab
text:
What’s next

A full race day, with a race picker, using the same tools.
Live Lynk model predictions for upcoming races.
Saved analyses, so a user can return to the questions they asked.

What I like most about this version is that the expensive parts of the original (the servers, the database bill, the hosted model) turned out to be optional. A horseplayer with a laptop can now run a racing analyst that knows a quarter of a million races, and it costs nothing to ask it a question.

title: One Race, One Winner
text:
Most machine learning tutorials and AutoML tools start from a table where every row is an example and the label is yes or no. A horse race fits into that table easily: one row per horse, label 1 if it won, 0 if it lost. My first generation of models at Lynk were built exactly like that, as per-horse classifiers.
However, a horse race is not a set of independent yes or no questions. Exactly one horse wins, and whether a horse wins depends entirely on who else is in the race. A horse that would be the favorite against a weak field is a longshot against a strong one, without anything about the horse changing.
Problem statement: does it matter whether the model is set up as binary classification (does this horse win?) or as multiclass classification over the field (which horse in this race wins?), and if so, how much and why?

title: One Race, One Winner
text:
Data
Source: the same Daily Racing Form result charts behind the fundamental model paper (Daily Racing Form, n.d.). The experiment uses 1.32 million starters from 2019 to 2023, which is every North American thoroughbred race over five years.
Features: only the fundamental (no odds) features, built strictly from races before each race. I split them into two sets:

Absolute (174 features): speed figures, finishes, class, connections, freshness and fit, without any comparison to today’s field.
Full (239 features): the same plus the hand-built field-relative versions, such as a horse’s rank in the race and its gap to the best figure in the field.

Splits: train on January 2019 to June 2022, stop training on July to December 2022, and score every race in 2023, a year neither model has seen.

title: One Race, One Winner
text:
Approach

Two ways to frame the same race
Binary classification scores each horse on its own with the logistic function, \(p_i = \sigma(s_i)\), and trains on the binary log-loss
\[
\mathcal{L}_\text{binary} = -\sum_i \big[\, y_i \log p_i + (1 - y_i) \log (1 - p_i) \,\big].
\]
Nothing forces the probabilities in a race to add up to one. A common fix is to divide each race’s probabilities by their sum after the model is trained, which I test below as “binary, normalized after”.
Multiclass classification treats the race as one choice among its starters. Each horse still gets a strength score \(s_i\), but the probabilities come from comparing the scores inside the race:
\[
p_i = \frac{e^{s_i}}{\sum_{j \in \text{race}} e^{s_j}}, \qquad
\mathcal{L}_\text{multiclass} = -\sum_{\text{races}} \log p_{\text{winner}}.
\]
This is the conditional logit (McFadden 1974), the model Bolton and Chapman (1986) and Benter (1994) used for handicapping, and the same idea as listwise learning to rank (Cao et al. 2007). The number of classes changes from race to race (it is the field size), which is why standard multiclass classifiers with a fixed number of classes do not fit and a custom objective is needed.






Figure 1: The same race scored both ways. The binary model’s probabilities add up to whatever they add up to. The multiclass model’s add up to one, so raising one horse lowers the rest.





Why the objective changes what the model learns
The difference shows up in the gradient, the signal each training example sends back to the trees. For a horse that lost, the binary gradient is just \(p_i\): “this horse’s own probability was too high”. It does not depend on the rivals at all. The multiclass gradient is \(p_i - y_i\) where \(p_i\) already depends on every rival’s score: “this horse’s probability was too high relative to this field”. Every training race becomes a lesson in comparison.
Think of it like grading on a curve. The binary model grades every horse on an absolute scale, as if it were running against a stopwatch. The multiclass model grades every horse against the other horses in the room, which is how a race is actually decided.


The experiment
To isolate the effect of the framing, I changed one thing at a time:

Model: LightGBM gradient boosted trees (Ke et al. 2017) with identical settings (learning rate 0.05, 63 leaves, at least 300 rows per leaf) and early stopping. The only difference is the objective: binary log-loss or the within-race softmax.
Normalization: the binary model is scored twice, once as is and once with its probabilities rescaled to sum to one in each race.
Feature sets: both objectives are trained on the absolute set and on the full set, so I can see how much of the field comparison each one learns by itself.
Training size: both objectives are also retrained on the last 6, 12, 24 and 42 months before the stopping window.
Scoring: race log-loss, the average of \(-\log p\) for the actual winner, with a 95% interval from a bootstrap that resamples whole race days (Efron and Tibshirani 1993). Lower is better.

title: One Race, One Winner
text:
Results

Binary probabilities do not form a race






Figure 2: Sum of the raw binary probabilities in each 2023 race, by field size. They should all be exactly one.



Left alone, the binary model’s probabilities for a race summed to anywhere from 0.73 to 1.32 (5th to 95th percentile), and that was the better of the two feature sets. With absolute features only, the range was 0.54 to 1.53. The error is not random: in two-horse races the probabilities summed to 0.67 on average and in fields of twelve or more to 1.07. In other words, the binary model systematically underrates horses in small fields and overrates horses in big fields, because it never learned that the number of rivals matters.
Normalizing after the fact fixes the sums. It also improves the log-loss a lot (from 1.7784 to 1.7243 with absolute features). However, it cannot fix what the model learned during training, which is where the multiclass objective earns its keep.


The headline

With the same raw features, switching the objective gained 0.025. For reference, that means the multiclass model puts about 2.5% more probability on the eventual winner, on average, across all 34,458 races in 2023. That is nearly four times the gain from the best fundamental feature family I built (pace and classic handicapping, +0.0066) and nearly three times the gain from blending in a neural network. A one-line configuration change beat weeks of feature engineering.


The multiclass model learns the comparison on its own
The most interesting result is how the two framings interact with the field-relative features:

Adding hand-built field-relative features improved the binary model by 0.020.
The same features improved the multiclass model by only 0.0024.
The multiclass model with absolute features only (1.6994) beat the binary model with all the field-relative features (1.7040) by 0.0046 (interval +0.0021 to +0.0072).

The point is that the comparisons I spent weeks hand-building (rank in the race, gap to the best figure, standardized values within the field) are mostly things the multiclass objective figures out by itself, because every gradient it sees is already a comparison. The binary model needs them spelled out and still falls short.


Bigger fields, bigger gains






Figure 4: Multiclass gain over normalized binary by field size, full feature set (thousandths of log-loss).



The advantage grows with the number of rivals: +0.0047 in fields of six or fewer, +0.0073 in fields of seven or eight, +0.0096 in nine or ten and +0.0111 in fields of eleven or more. That is what the theory predicts. The more horses in a race, the more the outcome depends on the field rather than on the horse alone, and the more a model that only grades on an absolute scale gives up.


Half the data






Figure 5: Race log-loss on 2023 by months of training data, full feature set.



The multiclass model was better at every training size I tried: 6, 12, 24 and 42 months. Trained on 24 months it scored 1.7019, already better than the binary model trained on all 42 months (1.7040). Every race teaches the multiclass model something about every horse in it, so it extracts more from the same data.


Where it does not help
Picking the winner barely changes. The top pick won 33.6% of 2023 races with the multiclass model and 32.8% with the binary model on absolute features, and the two were within 0.2 points of each other on the full set (33.3% versus 33.5%, slightly in the binary model’s favor). The gain is almost entirely in the quality of the probabilities across the whole field: how much the 15% horse and the 4% horse really deserve.
For a bettor that is the part that matters. A bet is only worth making when the model’s probability differs from the price, and the Kelly stake is sized directly from that probability (Kelly 1956). A model that picks the same winners with better probabilities finds better prices and sizes them better, which is why I agree with Walsh and Joshi (2024) that betting models should be judged on calibration and log-loss, not accuracy.

Verdict: framing the race as one multiclass choice instead of many binary questions was worth +0.025 in log-loss on identical data, more than any feature I ever built. It learns the comparison against the field on its own, helps most in big fields and needs about half the data. It does not pick more winners. It prices them better, and pricing is the whole game.

title: One Race, One Winner
text:
Limitations

One market, one model family. This is North American thoroughbred racing with gradient boosted trees. I expect the result to hold for any one-winner event (the neural network in the fundamental paper uses the same within-race softmax), but I have only measured it here.
A well-engineered binary model closes most of the gap. With full field-relative features the difference falls from 0.025 to 0.007. It is still significant and still large in betting terms, but most of what the multiclass objective does can be approximated by enough feature engineering.
It needs a custom objective. Off-the-shelf multiclass classifiers assume a fixed number of classes. The race softmax has to be written as a custom objective, which is one reason so many models default to binary. The Lynk framework ships one (GroupSoftmaxObjective and fit_group_softmax).
Winners only. This framing models the winner. Place, show and exotic bets need the full finishing order, which takes Harville-style or staged models on top (Harville 1973; Lo et al. 1995).

title: One Race, One Winner
text:
What’s next

A listwise objective over the top three finishers (a Plackett-Luce likelihood (Plackett 1975)) instead of the winner only, so the model is trained directly for place, show and exacta pricing.
The same head-to-head in other one-winner markets: three-way soccer results, golf and futures markets.
Combining the race softmax with the market’s odds as a starting point, which is how the framework’s market models are built.

I think the broader lesson goes beyond racing. Before reaching for a better model or more features, it is worth asking whether the problem is framed the way the world actually works. In a race, one horse wins, and the model should know that.

title: One Race, One Winner
text:
Reproducing this
The race softmax objective is lynk.core.models.GroupSoftmaxObjective in the Lynk repository. A minimal version of the comparison on the synthetic racing circuit:
from lynk.core.models import fit_group_softmax, predict_group_softmax
from lynk.core.metrics import group_log_loss

# multiclass: probabilities compete within each race
booster = fit_group_softmax(X_train, won_train, race_id_train, X_stop, won_stop, race_id_stop)
p = predict_group_softmax(booster, X_test, race_id_test)
print(group_log_loss(p, won_test, race_id_test))

title: Sizing the Bet
text:
Suppose a model says a horse has a 25% chance to win and the tote board shows 4-1, a $5.00 payout per $1. The bet has an edge: \(0.25 \times 5 - 1 = +25\%\) per dollar. How much should I bet?
Bet too little and the edge does nothing for the bankroll. Bet too much and a normal losing streak wipes it out, even though every single bet had positive expected value. In a pari-mutuel pool there is a third trap: bet enough and my own money drives the payout down until the edge is gone.
Problem statement: turn model probabilities into stakes that grow the bankroll as fast as possible without unacceptable risk, in markets where the price depends on the bet.
The rest of this paper climbs a ladder. Each step fixes one thing the previous step ignored.

text:
Step 1: The Kelly criterion
Kelly (1956) asked how a gambler with an edge should size bets to make wealth grow as fast as possible over many bets. The answer is to maximize the expected logarithm of wealth, because log wealth adds up across bets while wealth multiplies.
For one bet with win probability \(p\) and decimal odds \(o\) (net payout \(b = o - 1\) per dollar), staking a fraction \(f\) of the bankroll gives expected log growth
\[
G(f) = p \log(1 + f b) + (1 - p) \log(1 - f).
\]
Setting \(G'(f) = 0\) gives the Kelly fraction
\[
f^* = \frac{p b - (1 - p)}{b}.
\]
For example, the 25% horse at 4-1 gives \(f^* = (0.25 \times 4 - 0.75) / 4 = 6.25\%\) of the bankroll.






Figure 1: Expected log growth per bet for the 25% horse at 4-1. Growth peaks at full Kelly, half Kelly keeps most of it, and twice Kelly almost erases it.



The curve has a shape every bettor should memorize. Half Kelly keeps three quarters of the growth (0.56% versus 0.74% per bet). Twice Kelly keeps almost none (0.12%), and a little past that the growth turns negative: the bankroll shrinks over time even though every bet has a 25% edge. Over-betting is not just riskier, it is slower.
In the Lynk framework this is lynk.core.kelly.kelly_fraction(p, decimal_odds), and expected_log_growth draws the curve.

text:
Step 2: Fractional Kelly
Kelly assumes the probabilities are exactly right. They never are. If the model says 25% but the truth is 23%, the true Kelly stake is 3.75%, and betting 6.25% is already 1.7 times too much.
I simulated 1,000 bets on that horse, 2,000 times, where the model believes 25% and the truth is 23%.

This is why practitioners bet a fraction of Kelly (MacLean et al. 2011; Uhrı́n et al. 2021), and why Baker and McHale (2013) show that shrinking the Kelly stake is the right response to estimation error. Walsh and Joshi (2024) make the related point that for betting, a model should be chosen on calibration, not accuracy: Kelly sizes on the probability itself, so a miscalibrated probability is a mis-sized bet.

title: Sizing the Bet
text:
Step 3: Mutually exclusive outcomes
In a horse race only one horse can win, so bets on two horses in the same race are not independent. Losing on one horse often means winning on another. Kelly (1956) solved this case too, and Smoczynski and Tomkins (2010) gave an explicit algorithm:

Rank horses by expected return \(p_i o_i\).
Add horses to the betting set \(S\) while the next horse’s expected return beats the reserve rate \(R(S) = \dfrac{1 - \sum_{i \in S} p_i}{1 - \sum_{i \in S} 1/o_i}\).
Bet \(f_i = p_i - R / o_i\) on every horse in \(S\) and keep the rest.

title: Sizing the Bet
section: Step 4: My own money moves the price
text:
Step 4: My own money moves the price
Everything so far assumed fixed odds. A pari-mutuel pool is different: all the money bet on a race goes into one pot, the track takes its cut (the takeout \(t\)), and the rest is split among the winning tickets. If the pool total is \(T\), the money already on my horse is \(m\) and I add a stake \(s\), my payout per dollar is
\[
\text{payout}(s) = (1 - t) \, \frac{T + s}{m + s}.
\]
My stake goes into the denominator, so my own bet lowers my own price. Expected profit in dollars is
\[
\text{EV}(s) = p \, s \, \text{payout}(s) - s,
\]
which rises, peaks and then falls. Isaacs (1953) found the peak. Setting \(\text{EV}'(s) = 0\) and solving the quadratic gives the maximum expected value bet
\[
s^{*} = -m + \sqrt{\frac{a \, m \, (T - m)}{1 - a}}, \qquad a = p(1 - t).
\]
(Lynk extends it with a rebate \(r\) by replacing \(1 - a\) with \(1 - r - a\).)






Figure 3: Expected profit versus stake for the 25% horse in a $100,000 pool with $15,000 already on it and a 17% takeout.



For example, with $100,000 in the pool and $15,000 on my horse, the edge at a tiny stake is +38%. The best I can do is bet $3,271 for $565 of expected profit, at which point my own money has cut the payout from 5.53 to 4.69. Betting $7,000 earns nothing, and past that every extra dollar loses money. The point is that in a pool, the right question is not only “is this a good bet?” but “how much of this bet can the pool absorb?”.
The 2/3 cap: I never bet more than two thirds of the max-EV stake, a rule Benter (1994) described. At two thirds ($2,181) the expected profit is still $510, 90% of the maximum, for one third less money at risk. Lynk implements this as max_ev_bet and cap_at_max_ev.

title: Sizing the Bet
section: Step 5: Price at the odds that pay, not the odds on the screen
text:
Step 5: Price at the odds that pay, not the odds on the screen
Pari-mutuel odds keep moving until betting closes, and the payout is set by the final pool. A large share of the money arrives in the last minutes, and much of it is well informed (Asch et al. 1982). Recent work on interim odds shows that late odds movement predicts returns even after controlling for the final odds (Hanyu et al. 2025). The practical consequence: late money tends to pile onto the horses that go on to win, so a winner’s final payout is usually lower than the payout I saw when I bet.






Figure 4: In the synthetic racing circuit, horses that went on to win gained money share after the decision snapshot, while the field as a whole did not.



In the Lynk synthetic circuit, winners’ final money share rose about 4% after the decision time while the average horse’s did not move, so a winner paid about 4% less than the screen promised. My late-money simulator is built around exactly this effect, and ignoring it is enough to turn apparent edges into losses. So the expected value of a win bet has to be priced as
\[
\text{EV} = p \cdot \mathbb{E}[\text{payout} \mid \text{horse wins}] - 1,
\]
using a model of the final pool, conditional on the horse winning, not the current odds. Two lessons from building this:

A late-money simulator is part of the probability model. Forecasting where each horse’s price will close after the bet is placed is a model in its own right, and I built one for exactly that job.
Price consistently. If the probability model uses the late-money simulator, the payout must use the same simulator. When I upgraded the simulator for probabilities but kept the old version for payouts, the strategy got worse at every setting. Making them consistent fixed it.

title: Sizing the Bet
text:
Step 6: The portfolio solver
A single race can be bet through several pools at once: win, place (top two), show (top three), exacta (first and second in order) and the first leg of a daily double. Each pool has its own takeout, its own money and its own winners, and my money moves each pool’s prices separately. Sizing them one at a time misses the hedges between them and double counts risk.
Formulation: list every possible result of the race as a scenario \(k\) with probability \(\pi_k\). For three places that is every ordered top three, whose probabilities come from the win model through the discounted Harville formula (Harville 1973; Lo et al. 1995), which corrects plain Harville’s tendency to overrate favorites for second and third. (I compared it with the Henery (1981) and Stern (1990) models, and a learned second-place model beat all three, so the framework keeps the scenario builder pluggable.) For a pool with \(n_k\) winning outcomes in scenario \(k\) (one for win and exacta, two for place, three for show), my payout from that pool is
\[
\text{payout}_k(x) = \sum_{w \in \text{winners}} x_w \left(1 + \frac{\Pi_k(x)}{n_k (m_w + x_w)}\right), \qquad
\Pi_k(x) = (1 - t)(T + X) - \sum_{u \in \text{winners}} (m_u + x_u)
\]
where \(X\) is my total stake in the pool. Wealth in scenario \(k\) is the bankroll, minus all stakes, plus every pool’s payout, plus rebates, and the solver maximizes
\[
\max_{x \ge 0} \; \sum_k \pi_k \log \text{wealth}_k(x).
\]
Each payout is a concave function of the stakes, so the whole problem is concave and the solver finds the global optimum. I give it exact gradients and solve with L-BFGS-B.
One lesson cost me a day: the first version optimized stakes in dollars. With a $10,000 bankroll, the gradient of log wealth is about one millionth per dollar, and the solver stopped at its starting point, reporting success. Optimizing bankroll fractions instead fixed it. Lynk builds that in.






Figure 5: The same race solved three ways. Adding the place pool doubles expected growth. The exacta result is a warning, not a win (see below).



On a six-horse example, win-only betting earns 34 basis points of expected log growth on two bets. Adding the place pool, where my favorite value horse is underbet, doubles that to 68 basis points. Adding the exacta jumps to 113 basis points across 17 bets, and that is exactly the result not to trust. In this example the exacta pool was built from a different finishing model than my probabilities, so the solver sees edges that are really a disagreement between two models. A joint optimizer amplifies whichever pool’s expected values are most optimistic.
That is what happened in my real research too. Solved jointly across win, place, show and exacta, the optimizer put most of its money into the pools whose predicted edges were least calibrated, and it lost money in validation while the same engine restricted to the win pool made money. The rule I follow now: a pool only enters the portfolio after its predicted expected values are shown to be calibrated out of sample. The solver is a powerful tool, and the calibration gate is what keeps it honest.
In Lynk this is lynk.core.portfolio.optimize_portfolio, with Pool and Scenario objects, and lynk.horse_racing.bets.multi_pool_race_bets builds the scenarios for a race.

title: Sizing the Bet
text:
Step 7: Risk-constrained Kelly
Fractional Kelly controls risk indirectly. Busseti, Ryu and Boyd (2016) state the risk limit directly: maximize expected log growth subject to
\[
\sum_k \pi_k \, \text{wealth}_k^{-\lambda} \le 1, \qquad \lambda = \frac{\log \beta}{\log \alpha},
\]
which guarantees that the probability of wealth ever falling to a fraction \(\alpha\) of its starting value is at most \(\beta\). The problem stays convex.

title: Sizing the Bet
text:
Evaluating a sizing rule honestly
Sizing rules have settings (an edge cutoff, a Kelly fraction), and choosing them on the same data used to report results is a quiet form of overfitting. Every strategy in my research follows the same protocol:

Choose on validation, score test once. The rule is written down first: among settings with at least 300 bets, pick the highest validation log growth, and only bet if it is positive. Then the test period is scored a single time.
Report intervals, not points. Returns get a 95% interval from resampling whole race days (Künsch 1989).
Separate the edge from the rebate. Rebates (a share of turnover returned by the betting platform) can be most of the margin in pari-mutuel betting (Ziemba 2023), so I always report returns before and after rebates.
Measure capacity. Because my money moves the price, profit rises with bet size, peaks and falls. The size where it peaks is part of the strategy, not an afterthought.

title: Sizing the Bet
text:
Limitations

The solver trusts its scenarios. If the finish-order probabilities or the pool forecasts are wrong, the solver will confidently size wrong bets. Calibration checks have to come first.
One race at a time. The solver handles all pools in one race, but not correlations across races or across a day’s card beyond what fractional Kelly and the drawdown constraint absorb.
Late money is forecast, not known. The final pool is uncertain when the bet is placed. The current framework uses the forecast’s mean; carrying its uncertainty into the solver is a natural extension (Metel 2017).
Execution is outside the math. Some tracks stop large automated bettors one or two minutes before post, and that changes which snapshot a strategy can use.

title: Sizing the Bet
text:
What’s next

Carry the uncertainty of the late-money forecast into the solver as extra scenarios.
Add multi-race pools (daily double, Pick 3) to the portfolio solver with the same calibration gate.
Extend the same solver to fixed-odds sports markets, where the impact term disappears but the correlation structure gets richer.

The math in this paper fits on a few pages, and it is all implemented, tested and documented in the Lynk framework. I hope it saves the next person the day I spent watching a solver stop at its starting point.

title: Cooper Huston
text:
Passion project: quantitative wagering
Lynk started as a company and is now the project I keep coming back to. Horse racing is one of the best laboratories I know for quantitative finance. Every price is public, every result is final, the fees are posted, and the market is pari-mutuel, meaning everyone bets against each other in a shared pool while the track takes a cut. That makes it a clean place to ask the hard questions: is the crowd’s price efficient, where is it wrong, and how much can you bet before your own money moves the price against you?
The research below covers 648,670 races from 2012 to 2025, which is roughly 130 races a day, every day, for fourteen years. Each paper follows the same structure I use for every project: the problem, the data, the approach, the results, what the work does not do yet and where it goes next.


Handicapping Without the Tote
What actually predicts a horse race when you are not allowed to look at the betting odds: feature families, walk-forward results from 2019 to 2025, a neural network that reads the whole field and online ratings for trainers, jockeys and sires.


One Race, One Winner
Why framing the problem as “which horse in this race wins” instead of “does this horse win” was one of the most valuable decisions in the whole project, tested head to head on the same data.


Sizing the Bet
From the one-line Kelly formula to a nonlinear solver that sizes bets across win, place, show and exacta pools while accounting for how my own money moves the price.


Lynk: the code
The open-source Python framework that came out of this research: probabilities, Kelly sizing, pari-mutuel math, leakage-safe backtesting and a horse racing module, built so new markets can plug into the same core.


A note on scope: these papers describe methods and the fundamental (no odds) model in full. Proprietary models, specific betting strategies and their returns are intentionally left out.

title: Handicapping Without the Tote
text:
Every horse race comes with a crowd. By post time thousands of bettors have put money on each horse, and the tote board turns that money into odds. Those odds are a strong forecast. However, they are also the thing I want to beat, so a model that leans on them only learns to agree with the crowd.
Problem statement: build the best possible model of who wins a horse race using only what was knowable before the race from the horses’ past performances, and nothing from the betting on the race itself.
There are two practical reasons to want this model on its own:

It is an independent second opinion. A betting model works by finding where the crowd is wrong. A model that formed its view without the crowd is the cleanest source of disagreement (Benter 1994).
Some bets need a probability before any odds exist. For a daily double or a Pick 3, the later races have no win pool yet when the bet is placed, so the only usable forecast for those legs is a fundamental one.

title: Handicapping Without the Tote
text:
Data
Source: Daily Racing Form result charts for North American thoroughbred racing from 2012 to 2025: 72,884 chart files covering 648,670 races and 5.58 million starters. For reference, that is about 130 races a day, every day, for fourteen years. If you watched every one back to back at two minutes a race it would take two and a half years without sleeping.
Each chart records the race conditions (track, surface, distance, class, purse), every starter’s connections (trainer, jockey, owner, sire, dam), equipment and medication, and the running of the race: the position and lengths behind at each point of call, the final time, the speed figure, the official finish and the payoffs (Daily Racing Form, n.d.).
The leakage rule: a chart is written after the race, so everything in it is post-race information. I only use chart data in two ways:

As history for later races. A horse’s speed figure from its last start is a feature for its next start. Connection records (a trainer’s wins) use a trailing window that ends the day before the race.
As the label. Who won today is the target, never an input.

Same-day features (for example, how a jockey has done in earlier races on today’s card) only use races that were already official before the race being predicted.
What is not in the data: workouts, veterinary records, trip notes in structured form, and anything from the betting on the race being predicted. The morning line (the track handicapper’s odds line) is available, and I tested it separately, but it is an odds line, so I keep it out of the fundamental model on purpose.
The splits: I use a walk-forward design. To predict year Y, the model trains on races from 2016 up to the middle of year Y-1, uses the last six months of Y-1 to decide when to stop training, and then predicts all of year Y. It never sees year Y before it predicts it. Random train/test splits are the most common mistake in sports modeling: they let horses from the same race and the same day sit on both sides of the split, which leaks the answer and makes the model look much better than it is (Kaufman et al. 2012; Roberts et al. 2017).

title: Handicapping Without the Tote
text:
Approach

The model thinks in races, not horses
A horse race has exactly one winner, so the model should produce probabilities that add up to one within each race. I use the conditional logit, the same structure Bolton and Chapman (1986) and Benter (1994) used for handicapping, which goes back to McFadden’s choice models (1974):
\[
P(\text{horse } i \text{ wins}) = \frac{e^{s_i}}{\sum_{j \in \text{race}} e^{s_j}}
\]
Each horse gets a strength score \(s_i\), and the probabilities come from comparing those scores within the race. Adding a strong rival automatically lowers everyone else’s chance. The scores come from gradient boosted trees (Friedman 2001; Ke et al. 2017) trained with a custom objective that minimizes this within-race log-loss directly.
How I score models: race log-loss, the average of \(-\log p\) for the probability the model gave the actual winner. Lower is better. A model that gives the winner 25% scores 1.39 on that race, 40% scores 0.92. Differences of 0.002 to 0.02 sound tiny, but a gain of 0.02 means the model puts about 2% more probability on the eventual winner on average, across every race it ever predicts. Every gain below is measured with a 95% confidence interval from a bootstrap that resamples whole race days, since races on the same day share tracks, weather and surface conditions (Efron and Tibshirani 1993; Künsch 1989).


Feature families
I built about 250 features, grouped into families. Every one is built from earlier races only.



Table 1: The fundamental feature families. Past-race closing prices come from the official charts and are only ever used as history.










Family
What it captures
Examples

last figure, best of last 3, average of last 5, figure trend, best at today’s distance


Pace and running style
Where the horse is early and how it finishes, rebuilt from points of call
early and mid-race pace figures, stretch gains, lone speed, pace scenario of today’s field


Finish history
Results, not just times
finish position, lengths beaten, win and in-the-money rates, troubled trips


Class and earnings
The level the horse competes at
earnings per start, purse and claiming price versus recent races, class drop or rise


Track, surface and distance fit
Whether today suits the horse
record on this surface, at this track, at this distance, first time on turf, first route


Connections
The people around the horse
trainer and jockey win rates, trainer-jockey combination, trainer at this track, claim and layoff patterns, same-day form


Pedigree
What the bloodline does in these conditions
sire record by surface and distance, sire with first-time starters, dam’s other runners


Freshness and schedule
Readiness
days since last race, second start off a layoff, starts in the last year


Track bias and post
Today’s surface and the gate
same-day bias from earlier races on the card, post position record


Past odds and odds-adjusted form
How the horse has run relative to its past closing prices
average past closing probability, wins versus what its past prices expected


Horse profile
The animal
age, sex, gelding status, weight carried


Entity ratings
Long-run tendencies of trainers, jockeys, sires and owners (see below)
trainer at this track, jockey by surface and distance, sire by surface and distance






Field context: every key number also appears in a relative form: its rank in today’s field, its gap to the best horse in the race and its standardized value within the race. A 90 speed figure means little until you know whether the next best horse ran 70 or 95. These relative versions turned out to carry 43% of the model’s total importance, which is the clearest sign that horse racing is a contest against today’s field, not against a stopwatch.
Classic handicapping, rebuilt: speed figure handicapping (Beyer 1975) and pace handicapping (Quirin 1979) are decades old, but the charts only expose them indirectly. I rebuilt early, middle and late pace figures from the position and lengths behind at each point of call, measured against prior-year pars for the same track and distance. I also re-read the stretch call from the raw chart files, because the standard parse dropped it.


A neural network that reads the whole field
Trees score each horse mostly on its own row. A race is a set of horses that interact: two speed horses will burn each other out, and a single closer benefits. To capture that I built a neural network with self-attention layers (Vaswani et al. 2017), the same mechanism language models use to relate words in a sentence, applied to the horses in a race.






Figure 1: The neural fundamental model. Each horse is encoded, attention layers let every horse see the rest of the field, and a softmax produces probabilities that sum to one.



The network alone was about as good as the trees. However, the two make different mistakes, so a fixed blend (half trees, a quarter each of two five-seed network ensembles) beat the trees by 0.006 to 0.010 in every single year from 2019 to 2025, with every confidence interval clear of zero. That consistency is the result I trust most in this whole project: a gain that shows up in seven separate years is not luck.


Entity ratings: separating the trainer from the jockey from the horse
The classic way to measure a trainer is a win-rate window: wins over the last 365 days, maybe compared with how often the trainer’s horses were expected to win. Win-rate windows have three problems:

Confounding. Top trainers use top jockeys on good horses, so a window credits all three with the same wins.
Small samples. A trainer with six starts off a layoff and two wins looks like a genius.
Wrong yardstick. Raw win rate says who is good. What I want to know is who is better than their horses’ prices suggest.

The ratings fix all three. Every past race is modeled as a conditional logit whose baseline is the race’s closing probabilities from the chart, plus an effect for each trainer, jockey, horse, owner and combinations such as trainer at a track, trainer off a layoff or after a claim, jockey by surface and distance, and sire by surface and distance (18 types in all). After each racing day, every effect is updated with that day’s results, and all of them are estimated together, so a trainer only gets credit for what the jockey and the horse do not explain.
Each rating carries its own uncertainty, like a Kalman filter (Kalman 1960) or a Glicko chess rating (Glickman 1999). The analogy that comes to mind is Elo for chess (Elo 1978), except every player also has an error bar: a surprising win moves a new trainer’s rating a lot and a veteran’s rating a little. Ratings used to predict a race on day D only include results through day D-1.

Each version improved on the last in every year, with one exception I explain below: v6 is slightly worse than v5 in 2019 and 2020. From v1 to v6 the model gained 0.016 to 0.021 per year. On the most recent unseen period (July 2024 to January 2025) the fundamental model’s top pick won 35.1% of races, against about 13% for a random horse in the average 7.5-horse field, with an AUC of 0.76.


Which families matter
I measure each family the same way: add it to the model, train on 2019 to mid-2022, stop on late 2022, and score every race in 2023, a year the model has never seen.






Figure 3: Gain from adding each feature family, scored on all 2023 races. Blue intervals are clear of zero. The morning line (orange) is an odds line, tested for reference and not used.



The verdicts:

Pace and classic handicapping is by far the biggest fundamental gain (+0.0066, interval +0.0047 to +0.0087). Rebuilding pace figures from the points of call was worth more than any other single idea.
Entity ratings (+0.0035), connections and same-day form (+0.0030), within-race ranks (+0.0026) and deeper horse history (+0.0024) are all real, with intervals clear of zero.
Pedigree, field shape, bias-adjusted last race and race-day announcements are not significant on top of everything else. They are not useless on their own, but the other families already carry their information.
The morning line would add +0.010, more than any fundamental family. That says a good human handicapper’s line still knows things the charts do not, which is useful to know. I keep it out because the point of this model is to be odds-free.







Figure 4: Share of the 2025 model’s total split gain by feature family.



Inside the model, class and earnings (20%) and connections (17%) carry the most weight, followed by surface and distance fit (10%) and speed figures (10%). Pedigree barely registers. Speed figures matter less than handicapping folklore suggests, because once the model knows the class level a horse competes at and how it finished, the raw time adds less.


What the ratings found






Figure 5: How much each entity type improves on the closing price when used alone (2016 to 2020).



Measured alone against the closing price, the most useful ratings were sire by surface and distance, jockey, jockey by surface and distance, jockey by price range and running style, and trainer by surface and distance. The horse’s own rating added almost nothing, which makes sense: the market watches horses closely, but it does not keep careful books on how a sire’s offspring handle a mile on turf. All 18 types together improved on the closing price by 0.0019 on 2021 to 2022 races that were never used for tuning.
The most interesting finding was about time. I let every rating drift, so a trainer could get hot or cold, and tuning chose almost no drift at all. In other words, the market misprices durable tendencies, not streaks. A trainer who is good with layoff horses stays good with layoff horses, while the hot trainer of the last month is already in the price.


What did not work

Language model trip notes. I had a local language model tag chart comments (blocked, wide, steadied) into eleven trip categories. A controlled test showed no gain (1.6908 versus 1.6905). The structured chart fields already carry that signal.
ECDF transforms, which turn each figure into a percentile of a historical distribution. No gain over the within-race ranks.
Hot and cold streaks for trainers and jockeys, as described above.
Bias-adjusted last race, which credits horses that ran against a track bias. Small and not significant.
Model tuning. Re-tuning the trees moved log-loss by less than 0.0005. Every real gain came from new information.


Verdict: the fundamental model improved by about 0.02 in log-loss across every year from 2019 to 2025, and almost all of that came from three ideas: rebuilt pace figures, field-relative features and the neural network blend. Entity ratings help the most recent years. Consistency across seven separate years is what makes me confident these are real gains and not a lucky test period.

title: Handicapping Without the Tote
text:
Limitations

The ratings are young in the early years. The ratings start in 2012, so the 2016 to 2018 training rows see immature ratings. That is why v6 is slightly worse than v5 in 2019 and 2020 and better from 2023 on. Ranking the ratings within each race should fix this, and it is the next experiment.
No workouts. Published workouts are one of the few pre-race facts a human handicapper uses that this model does not have, so I expect them to be the largest remaining gain.
One country, one breed. Everything here is North American thoroughbred racing. Harness racing and international racing have different structures.
2020 is an outlier. The pandemic year had closed tracks and unusual fields, and every version scores worst there. The walk-forward design handles it honestly, but it is a reminder that racing conditions shift.
Fundamentals alone do not beat the closing price. This model is a strong independent opinion, not a betting system. The bet sizing paper covers how a probability turns into a bet.

title: Handicapping Without the Tote
text:
What’s next

Within-race ranks of the entity ratings, to remove the early-year drift.
Workouts and structured trip information as new pre-race inputs.
A neural network trained on the ratings directly, instead of blending them in afterwards.
Porting the feature pipeline into the open Lynk framework, so anyone can run the same leakage-safe workflow on their own data.

I think the biggest takeaway is how far honest testing gets you. Every gain on this page held up on years the model had never seen, and that is the only kind of gain worth building on.

title: The Lynk Framework
text:
The research behind the fundamental model and bet sizing papers produced more than 80 scripts. They worked, but they were written for one dataset, one machine and one question at a time. Specifically, three things made them hard to reuse:

The good ideas were buried in the specific code. The pari-mutuel solver, the leakage rules and the rating system each lived inside a script that was also tied to one particular data source.
The safeguards were habits, not code. Date splits, lagged features and pre-registered strategy selection were things I remembered to do, which means they were things someone else could forget.
Nothing ran without proprietary data. The racing data behind the research is licensed and cannot be redistributed, so nobody else could run any of it.

Problem statement: turn the research into a framework that someone else can install, understand and extend to a new market in an afternoon, with the safeguards built into the functions rather than left to discipline.

title: The Lynk Framework
text:
Approach
I designed Lynk around six principles, each one a lesson from the research.

Events come first. Most wagering markets are groups of mutually exclusive outcomes: horses in a race, teams in a match, candidates in an election. Every probability, metric and sizing function in Lynk works on groups, so probabilities always sum to one inside an event.
Leakage-safe by construction. Features that use history take a date and only look backwards. Connection records end the day before the event. Ratings used on day D only include results through day D-1. Splits are by date, and there is an assertion that fails loudly when a feature was observed after the decision time.
The market is a baseline, not a feature. Models accept a baseline log-probability (for example the crowd’s odds) as a starting score and learn corrections to it, which is how the strongest models in the research were built (Benter 1994).
Prediction, pricing and sizing are separate layers. A model produces probabilities. A market module turns them into prices (payouts, takeout, own-money impact, breakage). The sizing layer decides stakes. Swapping one layer does not touch the others.
Honest evaluation is a function call. Results come with day-block bootstrap intervals, returns before and after rebates, drawdown, and a pre-registered selection rule, because those are what keep a backtest from lying.
Every example runs without proprietary data. A seeded synthetic racing circuit has the same structure and the same traps as real racing, including a crowd that misprices some trainers and smart late money.

The analogy that comes to mind is a full stack application. The core is the backend: it does not care what the market is. Each market module is a frontend that maps its own data and bet types onto that backend. Horse racing is the first frontend, and the next ones should only need a schema, a few features and their own bet types.

title: The Lynk Framework
text:
A walkthrough
The quickstart in examples/quickstart.py runs the whole research workflow on a simulated year of racing in about 15 seconds. These are the important steps, in the order the code runs them.
1. Simulate and validate the data. The schema check sorts races so every event’s rows are contiguous.
from lynk.horse_racing import synthetic, schema
races = schema.validate(synthetic.make_races(n_days=360, races_per_day=10, trainer_mispricing=0.35))
2. Build leakage-safe features. History is lagged, connection form ends the day before the race and every number gets a field-relative version.
from lynk.horse_racing import features
races = features.add_history_features(races, ['speed_figure', 'finish_pct'])
races = features.add_connection_form(races, 'trainer', window_days=180)
races = features.add_relative_features(races, ['speed_figure_mean3', 'speed_figure_best5'])
3. Rate the connections against past closing prices. The ratings are updated day by day, and the features for each race only use earlier days.
from lynk.core.ratings import OnlineRatings, EntityType
ratings = OnlineRatings([EntityType('trainer', ['trainer'], prior_variance=0.01),
                         EntityType('jockey', ['jockey'], prior_variance=0.005),
                         EntityType('trainer_track', ['trainer', 'track'], prior_variance=0.003)])
rated = ratings.run(races, 'race_id', 'date', 'won', offset_col='log_closing_p')
4. Split by date, fit a fundamental model and a market model. The market model starts from the crowd’s odds at decision time and learns corrections from the fundamental opinion and the ratings.
from lynk.core import validation
from lynk.core.models import fit_group_softmax, predict_group_softmax
races['split'] = validation.date_split(races.date, valid_start='2023-09-01', test_start='2023-11-01')
market = fit_group_softmax(train[cols], train.won, train.race_id, stop[cols], stop.won, stop.race_id,
                           init_score=train.log_crowd_p.values, init_score_valid=stop.log_crowd_p.values)
5. Bet, choose on validation, score test once. The strategy prices each horse at the forecast final odds, sizes with the pari-mutuel solver, caps at two thirds of the max-EV bet and settles at the diluted official payoff.
from lynk.core import backtest
from lynk.horse_racing import bets
grid = backtest.grid_search(make_ledger, settings, bankroll=10000.0)
best, active = validation.select_preregistered(grid, metric='log_growth', min_bets=100)
summary = backtest.summarize_ledger(test_ledger)

The ratings work. In this simulated world the crowd ignores part of every trainer’s skill, and the ratings recover it, improving on the closing prices by 0.013 per race.
The market model beats the odds it bets into (1.8883 versus 1.9201 on the test months), because it combines the crowd with information the crowd ignores.

title: The Lynk Framework
text:
Testing
The test suite checks the math, not just that the code runs. A few examples:

The portfolio gradient matches finite differences for every stake, so the solver’s exact gradients are right.
The closed-form max-EV bet matches a brute-force search over 20,000 stakes.
Mutually exclusive Kelly matches a numerical optimizer on a book with a realistic margin.
Ratings recover a planted trainer effect in simulated races and beat the offset they start from.
History features never see today’s race, connection form is zero on the first racing day, and the leakage assertion raises an error when a feature arrives after the decision time.

All 21 tests pass. They run with pytest from the repository root.

title: The Lynk Framework
text:
Adding a new market
The core never imports a market module, so a new market is a new folder next to horse_racing:

Write a schema that maps the market’s data onto events, outcomes, dates and a market snapshot.
Build features with the same rule: history only looks backwards. The core’s validation.assert_features_precede can guard the pipeline.
Describe the bet types as pools or fixed-odds bets. Fixed-odds markets use kelly_mutually_exclusive or kelly_scenarios directly. Pari-mutuel markets describe each pool with Pool and each result with Scenario, and the portfolio solver does the rest.
Add a synthetic generator so examples and tests run without proprietary data.

title: The Lynk Framework
text:
Limitations

This is version 0.1. The core is tested, but the horse racing module is a clean re-implementation of research code, not a production betting system.
No data connectors. Racing data is licensed, so the repository ships the schema and a synthetic circuit instead of parsers.
The late-money forecast is deliberately simple. My research stack has a learned late-money simulator that forecasts where each horse’s price will close. The framework ships a transparent default and leaves the simulator as the plug-in point it should be.
No live execution. Placing bets, rate limits and track cutoffs for automated bettors are outside the scope of the package.
Nothing here is betting advice. A positive backtest with an interval that includes zero is not proven, and the framework is built to say so.

title: The Lynk Framework
text:
What’s next

The late-money simulator and conditional payout model as first-class plug-ins.
Multi-race pools (daily double, Pick 3) in the portfolio solver.
A second market module, starting with fixed-odds sports exchanges, to prove the core is truly market-agnostic.
API reference pages generated from the docstrings.

Racing taught me most of what is in this package, but very little of it is really about horses. Probabilities that respect the event, prices that respect the pool, stakes that respect the bankroll and tests that respect the calendar apply to any market where people bet against each other. That is what Lynk is for.
